messages.subject: Cluster identification with pvclust
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Could anyone help me with the interpretation of  a cluster analysis?
I am doing an agglomerative hierarchical cluster analysis and I assessed the number of clusters to consider via the multiscale bootstrap resampling method available via pclust.
This method identifies 2 clusters, immediately at the first ramification. But in lower branches, there are several significant subclusters too. My question now is if in my analysis I can take into account the results from the subclusters too, or if only the 2 big clusters are to be considered.

Thanks in advance for any help!

Clara

messages.subject_clean: [StatForLing with R] Cluster identification with pvclust
messages.body_plain:
Well, clustering IS an exploratory tool so I don't see why one
wouldn't want to discuss whatever 'significant' clusters emerge.
Results like these reflect 'significant' effects on different levels
of granularity, which may or may not be interesting depending on your
question (or questions other researchers may have later) so I would
report them all as results and then focus my interpretation on those
results that bear (most) on my hypothes[ei]s.

Just my $0.02,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
-----------------------------------------------
University of California, Santa Barbara
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries

messages.subject: Re: [StatForLing with R] robust glm
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stefan,

thanks for the pointer. Yes, I found glmrob from robustbase. Btw, are there any linguist-friendly pointers on choosing the right method with this function or is it a matter of trial and error? Another question is about the residuals: They should be more or less normally distributed, if the fitting is good. How strict is this criterion? I think on corpus data a normality test will most likely fail ...

Thanks and greetings,
Anne

messages.subject: Re: [StatForLing with R] robust glm
messages.body_plain:
I haven't seen any linguist-friendly pointers, no. Jennifer
Larson-Hall has discussed robust methods in some overview papers but,
given that they are overview papers, they can of course not go very
deeply. Then, the Field, Miles, & Field book (2012? 2013?)
"Discoverving Statistics with R" discusses a few robust statistics
methods (all based in WRS, I think), but there's really not much.
Maybe Wilcox's books are the best places to start, they explain most
things really well.

Cheers,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
-----------------------------------------------
University of California, Santa Barbara
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries
